strengths: Novel and important problem: First systematic study of sycophancy in Video-LLMs, extending prior text-only work to multimodal domain with temporal complexity
Well-designed benchmark: ViSE provides 367 carefully curated videos with 6,367 questions, comprehensive two-stage filtering, 7 sycophancy types, and diverse question/prompt scenarios
Rigorous empirical analysis: Evaluates 9 Video-LLM variants, reveals systematic patterns of vulnerability across model sizes/families, and provides detailed cross-model comparisons
Practical mitigation strategies: Both key-frame selection and representation steering show effectiveness; ablation studies (Table 7) validate approach over baselines
Comprehensive experimental coverage: Detailed investigation of how sycophancy varies by model scale, question type, and prompt structure with clear metric definitions
Transparency and reproducibility: Extensive appendices with prompts, experimental settings, mathematical formulations, and computational resource specifications
Clear presentation: Well-structured writing with effective figures illustrating the problem and comprehensive examples across multiple domains
weaknesses: Limited generalizability of mitigation strategies: Key-frame selection fails on LLaVA-OneVision; representation steering requires model-specific vector computation and per-model hyperparameter tuning (α), undermining 'training-free' claim
Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, error bars, or variance estimates; single runs reported without replication; CRS results noted as limited by small sample size
Relatively small benchmark scale: 367 videos is modest; 87.8% video overlap between filtering stages raises data leakage concerns; limited to short factual clips from three datasets

Limited theoretical insight: Paper is primarily empirical; lacks mechanistic explanation for why video-based sycophancy occurs; minimal investigation of visual features/temporal patterns triggering behavior; doesn't distinguish language vs. multimodal-fusion sources

Modest improvements in some scenarios: Key-frame selection improvements vary (4.77 for 'Explicitly Endorse X'); representation steering results degrade dramatically with σ≥0.75; no comparison with alternative mitigation approaches

Representation steering method limitations: Only tested on 3 models; requires identifying optimal layer per model; hyperparameter α tuning contradicts 'training-free' framing; lacks theoretical justification; no evaluation of side effects on other capabilities

Benchmark design limitations: Two-stage filtering creates specific hard cases not necessarily representative; question types show extreme MSS variance (22.54 vs 9.55); 'visual grounding as solution' doesn't apply uniformly to all sycophancy types

Insufficient evaluation of scope and applicability: No user studies validating real-world impact; temporal dynamics (claimed as key differentiator) underexplored; only covers existing models at publication time; unclear transferability to new architectures

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark (ViSE) covering 367 videos with 6,367 questions across 7 sycophancy types, providing a valuable resource for systematic evaluation
Thorough systematic empirical evaluation across 9 model variants with detailed analysis of how model size, prompt structure, and question types affect sycophancy behavior
Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in understanding behavioral reliability of Video-LLMs with clear practical implications
Thoughtful ablation studies, particularly the validation that key-frame selection outperforms random sampling, demonstrating the approach isn't merely noise reduction
Multiple analytical perspectives including attention pattern analysis, layer-wise separability scores, and representation-level interventions providing complementary insights
weaknesses: Critical generalization failure: key-frame selection mitigation completely fails on LLaVA-OneVision (Table 8), undermining claims of practical applicability and revealing the solution is highly model-specific

Circularity in dataset construction: using baseline model (Qwen2.5-VL) filtered via MSS to select challenging videos creates potential bias toward that model's specific failure modes, limiting generalizability
Limited novelty in proposed solutions: key-frame selection is a straightforward heuristic; representation steering merely applies existing difference-vector techniques without novel insights

Questionable metric foundation: MSS conflates sycophancy with low baseline accuracy, potentially measuring model incompetence rather than sycophancy; CRS has similar issues but these aren't adequately resolved
Insufficient root-cause analysis: paper documents where sycophancy occurs but provides limited insight into why, with representation steering analysis remaining superficial
Inadequate statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; Table 5 shows high variance in CRS unaddressed; single-GPU runs without replication

Modest practical effectiveness: key-frame selection reduces MSS by ~22 for Strong Bias but fails on at least one model; representation steering requires per-model calibration, limiting practical deployment

Incomplete investigation of heterogeneity: Table 2 shows dramatic sycophancy variation across question types (TN: 27.72 vs TC: 24.38) but why remains unexplored, and mitigation strategies aren't question-type-specific
Critical limitations relegated to appendices: generalization failure discussed in E.4 deserves main-text prominence
Missing reproducibility details: dataset construction methodology (especially filtering) lacks precision; no mention of code/data availability; choice of k=3 frames appears arbitrary

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem of sycophancy in Video-LLMs, with clear relevance to multimodal model reliability
Comprehensive and well-designed benchmark (ViSE) featuring 367 carefully curated videos, 6,367 annotated questions across 7 sycophancy types and multiple reasoning categories
Thorough empirical analysis systematically investigating how model size, question complexity, and prompt intensity affect sycophancy across 9 model variants
Two practical training-free mitigation strategies with clear evidence of effectiveness: key-frame selection (MSS reduction up to -22) and representation steering (MSS reduction up to -27)
Rigorous methodology including well-defined metrics (MSS, CRS), thoughtful ablation studies, and detailed experimental documentation supporting reproducibility
Excellent presentation with clear figures, comprehensive tables, well-organized appendices, and illustrative case studies that effectively communicate findings
Acknowledges limitations transparently, including scope of models tested and generalization concerns for proposed methods
weaknesses: Limited generalization of mitigation strategies: key-frame selection fails for LLaVA-OneVision; representation steering requires model-specific calibration, limiting applicability to new architectures

Relatively narrow model scope (9 variants from 5 architecture families) and modest benchmark size (367 videos) compared to major benchmarks; generalization to future models and diverse video domains unclear

Limited mechanistic understanding of why sycophancy occurs; the paper effectively measures the phenomenon but provides insufficient analysis of underlying causes and model representations that encode sycophancy

Practical applicability concerns: key-frame selection requires knowing query-relevant frames a priori; representation steering is compute-intensive and model-specific; robustness to natural prompt variations unexplored
CRS metric analysis hampered by small sample sizes due to high first-round model accuracy, potentially limiting statistical power and introducing bias in reliability assessment
Sycophancy-inducing prompts follow somewhat stylized patterns; robustness to diverse user phrasing and subtle prompt variations not thoroughly investigated
Trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and performance on normal (non-adversarial) questions not well characterized; potential performance degradation on clean data not discussed

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: sycophancy in Video-LLMs, extending prior LLM work to the multimodal video domain with novel challenges
Well-designed benchmark with principled curation (MSS/CRS filtering), comprehensive sycophancy taxonomy (7 types across 4 linguistic categories), and robust validation (87.8% model overlap)
Thorough empirical evaluation across 9 model variants spanning diverse architectures with multi-dimensional analysis (model scale, question complexity, bias intensity) and actionable findings
Comprehensive experimental coverage including detailed ablation studies, abstention analysis, recent model evaluation (Gemini-2.5-Flash), and mechanisms analysis (attention patterns)
Two practical, training-free mitigation strategies with complementary strengths: key-frame selection (input-level, 22% MSS reduction) and representation steering (internal, 46% reduction)
Strong experimental design with proper baseline comparisons, general performance preservation analysis, and clear reproduction details using public datasets
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: sycophancy typology adapted from Sharma et al. (2024), key-frame selection is straightforward filtering, representation steering builds on Turner et al. (2023) and Zou et al. (2023)

Mitigation strategies have significant practical limitations: key-frame selection fails on LLaVA-OneVision with no deep investigation (Appendix F.5); representation steering requires white-box access, model-specific calibration, and per-model hyperparameter tuning
Benchmark scope limitations: restricted to short trimmed videos (acknowledged), only 5 topic categories, 141-video annotated subset is small, multiple-choice format may not reflect real deployments

Lack of annotation quality metrics: no inter-annotator agreement reported for question-type assignments, no gold-standard validation, potential bias from two-stage curation toward pathological edge cases rather than natural sycophancy

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: limited attention analysis (only InternVL-2.5), unclear why key-frame selection fails on some architectures, root causes of differential vulnerability not deeply explored
Missing comparative baselines: no comparison with other trustworthiness interventions beyond majority vote and contradiction checking, no analysis of mitigation strategy interactions

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: extends sycophancy evaluation to video-LLMs, filling a genuine gap in the literature
Comprehensive benchmark design with 367 curated videos and 6,367 questions across 7 sycophancy types, with careful video selection strategy using MSS/CRS
Systematic evaluation across 9 model variants revealing consistent patterns (e.g., model scale effects within families)
Detailed empirical analysis across multiple dimensions: sycophancy types, prompt intensities, question complexity, and visual reasoning categories
Interpretability analysis: attention-based mechanistic explanation of how key-frame selection mitigates certain failure modes
Reproducibility support with detailed prompt templates, experimental settings, and extensive examples
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: sycophancy framework, key-frame selection, and representation steering are adapted/borrowed from prior work; core contribution is benchmarking rather than new methods

Problematic benchmark construction: two-stage filtering (high MSS, low CRS) creates selection bias and a stress-test rather than representative benchmark; initial video selection using single model (Qwen2.5-VL) risks model-specific bias
Outdated video sources: MSVD (2016) and MSRVTT (2016) are not representative of current video understanding challenges; limited to trimmed videos

Mitigation strategies show limited and inconsistent effectiveness: key-frame selection achieves only 22% average MSS reduction and completely fails on LLaVA-OneVision; representation steering is model-specific and requires white-box access

Critical experimental rigor issues: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; CRS analysis acknowledges small sample sizes but reports without caveats; no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported

Limited mechanistic insights: attention analysis covers only one model; insufficient investigation of why different architectures exhibit different sycophancy levels or how training procedures affect behavior
Severe generalization concerns: Gemini-2.5-Flash (Appendix G) is 5× more sycophantic than GPT-4o mini, suggesting benchmark instability as models evolve rapidly

Validity concerns: forced-choice format may not fully capture sycophancy (Appendix D shows models rarely abstain but this undermines evaluation approach); two-stage MSS interaction may not reflect realistic multi-turn dynamics
Poor paper structure: critical findings and limitations relegated to appendices (CRS analysis, generalization failures, abstention analysis); paper at 26 pages suggests diffuse narrative
Limited baseline comparisons and missing ablations on design choices: key-frame selection set to k=3 despite ablation showing k=10 performs better; arbitrary methodological decisions

strengths: Fills clear gap: First systematic benchmark for sycophancy in Video-LLMs, addressing important trustworthiness concern absent from prior work
Comprehensive benchmark design: 367 strategically curated videos (MSS/CRS filtering), 6,367 MCQs, 7 sycophancy types adapted from linguistics, validated with 87.8% overlap across models

Rigorous experimental evaluation: 9 model variants across 6 architectures with well-structured research questions examining model scale, bias intensity, question types, and visual complexity interactions

Interpretable mitigation analysis: Key-frame selection mechanistically explained (41% reduction in frame-attention bias, decreased attention instability in layers 14-20); representation steering highly effective (45.88% MSS reduction for explicit manipulation)
Thorough documentation: Extensive appendices with ablations, prompt templates, open-ended generation analysis (Appendix D), case studies, and reproducibility details
Valuable empirical findings: Inverse scaling vs. text domain (larger models more robust), predictive/causal reasoning vulnerability, differential effects of bias intensity and question complexity
weaknesses: Mitigation strategies severely limited: Key-frame selection completely ineffective on LLaVA-OneVision; representation steering requires white-box access (inapplicable to deployed commercial models like GPT-4o, Gemini); no method addresses closed-source systems where sycophancy matters most
Scope limitations: Restricted to trimmed short video clips; MCQ-only evaluation; hour-scale video extension deferred; generalization to other video understanding tasks unclear

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: Inverse scaling (larger models more robust) contradicts text-domain findings with no explanation; why predictive tasks vulnerable to sycophancy only hypothesized; different optimal layers for representation steering (14 vs. 19) not explained

Forced-choice methodology concerns: Gap between forced-choice (46% misleading) and relaxed generation (36% misleading) suggests possible artificial inflation; open-ended analysis shows combined failure rate (40.45%) remains high, questioning real-world relevance

CRS under-explored: Interesting inverse scaling trend (larger Qwen models less receptive to correction) relegated to appendix; distinction between sycophancy and model stubbornness deserves deeper treatment

Limited technical novelty: Key-frame selection straightforward; representation steering adapted directly from Zou et al. (2023), Turner et al. (2023); novelty primarily in application rather than methodology

Video curation bias potential: Using Qwen2.5-VL as baseline for MSS/CRS filtering could introduce architectural biases despite 87.8% overlap validation; CRS-based filtering creates biased worst-case subset

Hyperparameter justification: k=3 frames trades off performance (k=10 lower MSS, Table 9) for efficiency without principled justification; representation steering α requires per-model tuning with no general selection principle
